ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Corruption in Passport Offices 
*261. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of large scale corruption in the Passport Offices in 
the country; and 
(b) what steps Government are taking to do away with touts in such offices? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MI NISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI 
AJIT KUMAR PANJA): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Government views reports of corruption in  passport offices with utmost seriousness. 
During the year 1999, 25.8 lakh passports were  issued from 28 passport offices and the 
reports of alleged corruption in the passport offices are very small in number as compared 
to the volume of passports issued. 
SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I should say that although my question 
relates to corruption in passport office the Minister's answer is very honest. He says that 
25 lakh passpc^ were issued during the year 1999, and the reports of corruption in tf. 
2 

[10 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
passport offices are very small in number as compared to the volume of passports issued. 
The only correction that he should make is that it is not very small, but it is total. And it is 
to such an extent that it is impossible to  even deposit the form in the passport office 
unless you go through the proper channel. Now it is on account of delay that the 
malpractices are occurring. And I have the figures given by the Government. As on 21st 
July, in Maharashtra, 30,000 passport applications were pending for more than 35 days; 
21,000 applications were pending in Punjab; in Tamil Nadu, the number was 25,000; and 
in Uttar Pradesh, again, it was 25,000. My quest ion to the hon. Minister is: If this is the 
case, then why does not the Government agree to open more passport offices? 
SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA: Si r, the opening of regional passport offices is dependent 
on the Report of the Standing Committee of Parliament, wherein, in 1994, they 
recommended that if the total applications in one specific area become 50,000 or more 
than that, a regional passport office would be opened. But realising the difficulties of the 
people, we have opened 20 more  passport application collection centres. The people can 
go there, their documents will be examined and the passport application forms will be 
accepted there. The delivery will take place by Registered Post. 
SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: In that case, will the Minister give a definite date by which 
this backlog will be cleared and will he also assure the House that this backlog will not be 
allowed to mount up? 
SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA: Sir, this is not the pendency or the backlog. The statement 
which the hon. Member has read out is about the pendency because of Police 
verification. We define pendency in our Ministry as one where Police verification is clear, 
the application otherwise is complete, but it is still remaining pending because the 
passport is yet to be written properly and delivered. These are figures where Police 
verification is still pending. Police verification should take three weeks time and the total 
period for issuance of a passport that we have envisaged is five weeks' in the case of a 
normal passport wherein the passport fee is Rs. 300. If it is under the Tatkal Scheme, we 
try to deliver it within ten days and, some times, even on the next day, depending on the 
exigencies, with a charge of Rs. 1800 (Rs. 300 plus Rs. 1500). The exceptions are three-fold. 
The first

without any extra charge.

2022. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state:

is not sufficient considering importance of agriculture in our economy;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI

international co-operation in the field of  agriculture. Agreements-Memorandum of

pests, plant diseases and weeds and spread of infective diseases on the territories of 
both the countries while trading in agricultural projects, animals, animal products, raw 
materials of animal origin and animal f eed. These kind of agreements facilitate 
development of India's trade in agricultu ral and veterinary products with these 
countries. 
India is an active member of several international organisations, such as, the 
United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Food 
Programme etc. India is also a benefi ciary of the programmes of all these

Recommendations of the expenditure re forms commission (ERQ) which require 
consultations with state Governments/Ministries/ Departments, etc. 
1. The State Governments will have to put in major efforts for identifying the 
BPL population, giving them ration card and reaching the benefits intended for them 
in a transparent manner. 
2. A national food security buffer stock of 10 million tonnes-4 million tonnes 
of wheat and 6 million tonnes of rice should be maintained at all times. 
3. The cost of holding the stocks in exce ss of the requirement for national food 
security and for PDS due to very ge nerous minimum support prices based 
procurement policy could be reflected in the Budget as producers' subsidy rather than 
consumer subsidy. 
4. Inducing the State Governments and the private sector to enter into the 
foodgrains trade— procurement, storage as we ll as including exports, in an organized 
and big way by moderating the increase in MSP effected every year. 
5. Freezing the MSP for paddy/rice and wheat in the 
forthcoming procurement seasons at the same level as fixed for the

last procurement season and accepting the prices recommended by a body of experts 
like the CACP without making further increases.

be allowed to procure, sell and also e xport upto 3 million tones of rice and 5 million 
of wheat every year and also that this policy will remain unchanged for at least 15 
years and that in the event of drop in foodgrains' production in any year, domestic 
consumption requirements would be met through imports. 
7. Move towards a procurement price in stead of minimum support price that 
will include the MSP as well as reasonable leve ls of taxes and other levies that can be 
imposed by the States, thus leaving it to th e States to decide on what they should 
retain by way of taxes and levies and what should be passed on to the farmers. 
8. (a) Encouragement to rice procurement through levy route. 
(b) There be only one rate as is the case with wheat and 
that be the Common variety alone.

standard may be announced befo re the coming season and levy 
percentage be fixed anywhere between 50% to 70% as the miller

10. Speedy action to be taken on all cost reduction measures in respect of the 
Food Corporation of India as may be r ecommended by the Administrative Staff 
College of India, which is currently undertaking a study to suggest ways and means of 
reducing the economic cost. 
11. Use of synthetic bag for procurement of rice. 
12. The States which distribute quantities larger than what is allocated under

Indo-European Union summit at Lisbon 
2075. SHRI R.P. GOE NKA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the major achievements of the two day Indo-European Union Summit led by the 
Hon'ble Prime Minister held at Lisbon, recently; and * • 
(b) the specific areas of trade and investment for which assurance, if any, were 
received or understanding was reached with different members of the European 
Union during the tour? 
120 

[10 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA): (a) The India- EU Summit held in Lisbon on June 28, 
2000 enabled both sides to review bilateral, regional and multilateral issues of mutual 
concern. * A major step forward was the agreement to forge a new strategic partnership 
in the 21st century founded on shared valu es and aspirations and characterised by 
enhanced and multifaceted cooperation. The India-EU Summit Declaration provides a 
blueprint for upgrading the relationship to a qualitatively higher level. An Agenda for 
Action which encompasses joint initiatives in the political, commercial and economic 
fields was also agreed upon. The Declaration commits India and the European Union to 
cooperate to prevent and combat terrorism and to meet the challenges arising from it in 
the regional and international context. India and the EU will also strive together for a 
Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism. 
(b) India and the EU have agreed that it is  essential to raise the level of bilateral 
trade and investment so that its full potential can be realised. The Summit 
Declaration makes specific reference to bilateral consultati ons on anticipated 
regulatory and other measures affecting the flow of trade with a view to resolving 
problems at an early stage. The EU has agreed to encourage larger flow of Foreign 
Direct Investment, especially in the infrastructure sector. It was agreed that a Joint 
working Group on Information Technology and Research and Development would 
also be set up.

-(c) whether Government will accord approval to these proposals early; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) to (d ) Government of Himachal Pradesh 
vide their Bill No. 4 of 1995 "The Employ ment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification 
of Vacancies) Himachal Pradesh (Amendment) Bill, 1995 desired to amend the 
Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959 which is 
a central Act, primarily with a view to make compulsory recruitment in public/private 
sector through employment exchanges. The Bill was passed by the Legislative 
Assembly of Himachal Pradesh and sent to the President of India for his assent. 
Government of India did not favour the Himachal Pradesh (Amendment) Bill 
being given assent by the President of India in view of the following:— 
(i) In the event of the Amendment taking the form of the law, the very basic 
structure of the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 
1959 will get changed because while under th e existing provisions it is compulsory 
only to notify the vacancies, in the changed situation it will become obligatory on the 
part of the employers to necessarily make  selection against the notified posts from 
amongst the candidates recommended by the employment Exchanges irrespective of 
whether the candidates recommended by the Employment Exchanges actually meet 
the requirements essential for filling up of such posts or not. 
(ii) The Amendment is also to the effect that prior approval of 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2000] 
the State Government authorities would be required to fill up vacancies in case 
Employment Exchanges fail to sponsor suitable candidates. 
In the fast changing liberalisation process on the economic front, such restrictive 
provisions will adversely affect the freedom of an enterprises in the public and private 
sector to manage their manpower efficiently. 
(iii) In the event of the proposed Amendment taking the shape of law in 
Himachal Pradesh, the possibility of some other State Governments coming up with 
similar proposals cannot be ruled out. As th e Act has been enacted by the Central 
Government, it is appropriate the various  provisions of the Act remain uniform 
throughout the country.

RAHMAN KHAN:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE 
MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) A Commission on Review of Administrative Laws was 
set up by the Government on 8 May, 1998 with the following terms of reference: 
(i) To undertake an overview of steps taken by different 
MinistriesDepartments for the review of  administrative laws, 
regulations and procedures administ ered by them, and the follow-up 
steps thereafter, for repeal and amendment. 
(ii) To identify, in consultation with  Ministries'Departments and client

one Department, or where they have a bearing on the effective working

sector, or where they have a bearing on industry and trade.

(iii) To examine, in the case of selected areas like environment, industry, trade 
and commerce, housing and real estate, specific changes in existing rules 
and procedures so as to make them objective, transparent and 
predictable.

repeal/amendments of laws^ regula tions and procedures, legislative 
process, etc. 
The Commission submitted its report on 30 September, 1998. 
The Commission, inter-alia, has mentioned in their report that the 'Licence Raj' 
may have been diluted because of recent indus trial policies, but 'Inspector Raj' is still 
thriving. The frequency of inspections vari es across States, depending on the number 
of laws and inspections enforced by the State Governments. 
The Commission recommended that the persistence of the inspector Raj' calls for 
review of the rationale for inspections and documentation under different Central and 
State Departments, the laws and practices governing inspections, and the need for the 
adoption of more efficient and transparen t surveillance and audit mechanisms. The 
Commission noted the efforts made by a numbe r of States to rationalise, consolidate, 
simplify and reduce forms and returns, to introduce single forms with multiple 
columns for different agencies, and reduc e the requirements for the submission of 
documentation. These need to be sustained and enlarged.

DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTR ATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC

AND PENSIONS AND MINISTER OF ST ATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE ): (a) The Planning Commission 
estimates the percentage of  persons living below poverty line at National and State

last such survey was conducted in 1993-94. As per the latest estimates of percentage of

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2000] 
Maharashtra lived below the povert y line in 1993-94. Since the 
National Sample Survey (NSS) data  on consumer expenditure are not 
available at district level, and as the Planning Commission estimates 
the poverty on the basis of the quinquennial consumer expenditure 
survey conducted by the Nationa l Sample Survey Organisation 
(NSSO), it is not possible to estimat e the incidence of poverty in the 
Adivasi districts.  
(b) to (e) There is a three-pronged actio n to alleviate and re duce the poverty in 
the country. These are (i) acceleration of  economic growth, (ii) human, and social 
development through literacy, education, health, nutrition, meeting of the minimum 
needs, elevation of social a nd economic status of the weaker  sections of the society, 
etc,, and (iii) dir ect attack on poverty through empl oyment and income generating 
programmes and assets-building for the poor. 
The increase in income of the people living below the poverty line occur from 
the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation of the poor 
arising from various anti-poverty programmes introduced from time to time by the 
Government for their upliftment. Since the Sixth Five Year Plan (1980—85), the 
Government has been implementing employ ment, and asset gene ration schemes for 
the upliftment of the people living below the poverty line. These schemes are mainly 
of two types, self-employment and wage employment. Integrated Rural Development 
Programme (IRDP) has been the major sel f-employment programme and it has been 
in operation in all the blocks of the country since 1980. The wage employment 
programme intially was National Rural Em ployment Programme (NREP) during the 
Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, another wage employment programmes under 
the name Rural Labour Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP) was 
introduced. Then in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched by merging 
the National Rural Employment Progra mme and the Rural Labour Employment 
Guarantee Programme, and it became the main wage-employment a programme. In 
addition, several programmes to help the poor  were also in operation until March, 
1999. These programme are Million Wells Scheme (MWS), Em ploment Assurance 
Scheme (EAS), Developmen t of Women and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), 
Training of Rural Youth for 
200 

[10 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Self-Employment (TRYSEM), Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans 
(SITRA). 
Form 1st April, 1999, these programme s, excepting EAS and JRY have been 
restructured into single self-employment programme called the Swarnajayanti Gram 
Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the prim ary objectives of focused approach to 
poverty alleviation, capita lising advantages of group lending, and overcoming the 
problems associated with multiplicity of  programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, 
Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has been restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi 
Yojana (JGSY) with the primary objective of creation of demand driven community 
village infrastructure including durable assets at the village level and assets to enable 
the rural poor to increase the opportunities  for sustained employment. Its secondary 
objective is generation of supplementary employment for the unemployed poor in the 
rural areas. The wage employment under th e programme is given to Below Poverty 
Lines (BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swarna Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the main 
poverty alleviation progamme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which has subsumed 
all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, viz. Nehru Rozgar Yojana 
(NRY), Urban Basic Service for the Poor (U BSP), Prime Minister's Integrated Urban 
Poverty Eradication Programme  (PMIUPEP), seeks to pr ovide gainful employment 
to unemployed or underemployed urban and educated up to IX standard for setting up 
self employment ventures or provision of  wage employment. The implementation of 
SJSRY is relying on suitable community structures on the UBSP pattern and delivery 
of inputs under this programme is thr ough the medium of Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs) and such community structure. 
It is not possible to isolate the impact of each of these factors on the income 
generation of the poor, and hence on the percentage of people living below the 
poverty line. However, as a result of the join t impact of these two factors, there has 
been a reduction in the percentage of people living below the poverty line in 
Maharashtra from 55.88 per cent in 1997-78 to 36.86 per cent in 1993-94.

2. The terms of reference of the National Statistical Commission are as follows: 
(i) To examine critically the deficiencies of the present statistical system in 
terms of timeliness, reliability and adequacy; 
(ii) To recommend measures to correct the deficiencies and revamp the statistical 
system to generate timely and reliable statistics for the purpose of policy and 
planning in Government at different levels of administrative structure; 
(iii) To recommend permanent and effective coordinating mechanism for ensuring 
integrated development of the decentralised statistical system in the country;

Programme Implementation (Statistics Wing) and other statistical units 
of the Government and to make recommendations on their staffing and 
training requirements to enable them to cope with the increase and 
development of statistical services; 
(vi) To examine the need for instituting st atistical audit of the range of services

MR. CHAIRMAN: I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away of Shri 
S. Nijalingappa, an eminent Gandhian, on the 8th August, 2000 at the age of 98.

RAJYA SABHA [10 AUGUST, 2000] 
An advocate by profession, Shri N ijalingappa was an active social and 
political worker. A veteran freedom fighter, he was imprisoned for two years for 
participating in the Quit India movement in 1942. He was associated with various 
social organizations in different capacities.  He worked for the formation of States on 
linguistic basis. He devot ed himself to the decentralisation of industry and 
development of villages and welfare of Sche duled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Even 
after retirement from active politics, he continued to provide leadership to 
cooperatives and continued his public life as a veritable watchdog and was known for 
his convictions. Shri Nijalingappa was a Me mber of the Mysore Legislative Council 
during 1937-38. He served as the President of the Constituent Assembly of Mysore. 
He also served as the Chief Minister of Erstwhile Mysore for four terms. He was also 
a Member of the Constituent Assembly dur ing 1948-50 and of Provisional Parliament 
during 1950-52. Shri Nijalingappa was a Member of the First Lok Sabha from 1952 to 
1956. 
In the passing away of Shri Nijalinga ppa, the country has lost an able 
administrator, a noted parliamentarian and a veteran freedom fighter. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Nijalingappa. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed.
